hook: Your Gujarat map hides a 96 kilometre creek that India and Pakistan still argue over, because the water around it keeps moving.
title: Why Kutch Is Stranger Than You Think
description:
Sir Creek is a tidal channel between Gujarat and Pakistan where India and Pakistan still disagree on where the border runs. This video explains why, and tours the strange land around it: a salt desert that turns into a sea, swimming camels, the Harappan city of Dholavira and an 1819 earthquake that raised a wall of land.

#SirCreek #Kutch #IndiaFacts
comment_prompt: Rann, camels or Dholavira: which is your pick?

chapters.title: A desert that turns into a sea
Camels that swim in the sea
The quake that built a wall
Sir Creek: a border in water

scenes.narration: Your Gujarat map hides a 96 kilometre creek that India and Pakistan still argue over, because the water around it keeps moving.
scenes.headline: Border in the water

scenes.narration: That border runs through mud and mangroves, where the water changes shape with every tide.
scenes.headline: Mud, mangroves, tides

scenes.narration: By the end of this video, you will see exactly why a single line on a map can be so hard to draw.
scenes.headline: Why the line is hard

scenes.narration: But first, the region around it is just as strange. It is called Kutch, and it is the largest district in India.
scenes.headline: Kutch, India's biggest district

scenes.narration: Here is what is coming: a desert that turns into a sea, camels that swim, and a city older than most countries.
scenes.headline: What is coming

scenes.narration: And an earthquake that built a wall across a river. Stay for the last one, because Sir Creek is the strangest of all.
scenes.headline: Save the best for last

scenes.narration: First, the White Rann. In winter it looks like a snowfield, a flat white plain of salt that runs all the way to the horizon.
scenes.headline: The White Rann

scenes.narration: But it is not snow. It is a salt marsh, and in the monsoon, water spreads over it until the plain becomes a shallow sea.
scenes.headline: Desert to sea

scenes.narration: Then the water dries up, the salt is left behind, and the white desert appears again. Same place, two completely different maps.
scenes.headline: Two maps, one place

scenes.narration: So a map of this place is never really finished. Whatever you draw in July is wrong by December.
scenes.headline: Never finished

scenes.narration: Keep that in mind. A land that flips between sea and desert is exactly where a border becomes hard to fix.
scenes.headline: Remember this

scenes.narration: Next, a fact that sounds fake. In Kutch, there is a breed of camel that swims in the sea.
scenes.headline: Camels that swim

scenes.narration: They are called Kharai camels. Kharai means salty, and these camels eat the leaves of mangroves growing on islands off the coast.
scenes.headline: Kharai camels

scenes.narration: During the monsoon, herds swim out to those mangrove islands and can stay there for days, eating.
scenes.headline: Swimming to islands

scenes.narration: Experts say they can swim about three kilometres through salt water. A camel, in the sea, paddling its way to lunch.
scenes.headline: Up to 3 km swim

scenes.narration: Local herding communities have looked after them for generations, but coastal industry has cut into the mangroves they depend on.
scenes.headline: Mangroves shrinking

scenes.narration: So the breed is now classed as threatened. A swimming camel sounds like a joke, but it is a real and fragile animal.
scenes.headline: A fragile animal

scenes.narration: Stranger things sit under the ground nearby. And one of them is a city that planned for every drop of rain.
scenes.headline: Something older nearby

scenes.narration: Dholavira. Imagine a city in the middle of a salt desert that was built around saving water.
scenes.headline: Dholavira

scenes.narration: It sits on an island in the Rann, and it is one of the great cities of the Harappan civilisation.
scenes.headline: A Harappan city

scenes.narration: UNESCO made it a World Heritage Site in 2021, the first Harappan site in India to get that honour.
scenes.headline: UNESCO site, 2021

scenes.narration: The people here built big stone reservoirs and channels to catch rain and store it, thousands of years ago.
scenes.headline: Stone water tanks

scenes.narration: The streets followed a plan, and the city was divided into separate parts. This was serious engineering.
scenes.headline: A planned city

scenes.narration: And it even had a signboard. Archaeologists found large letters of the Harappan script, and nobody has been able to read them.
scenes.headline: A sign nobody can read

scenes.narration: Think about that. A message from thousands of years ago, in a script still unread, in the middle of the Rann.
scenes.headline: Unread message

scenes.narration: If you like strange places and facts that sound fake but are true, subscribe. We post a new one every day.
scenes.headline: Subscribe for more

scenes.narration: The next one explains why this whole region has the shape it does. It happened on a single day in 1819.
scenes.headline: One day in 1819

scenes.narration: In June 1819, a huge earthquake hit Kutch. Scientists estimate its magnitude at about seven point seven.
scenes.headline: June 1819 earthquake

scenes.narration: A long ridge of land rose up, and local people named it Allah Bund, which means the dam of God.
scenes.headline: Allah Bund

scenes.narration: It ran for many kilometres across the old river channels and dammed the water that used to flow through them.
scenes.headline: A wall across a river

scenes.narration: Nearby, Sindri Fort partly sank, and the ground around it filled with water to form a lake.
scenes.headline: A fort sinks

scenes.narration: Some accounts say the lower mouth of that river became a tidal inlet, and that inlet is now called Kori Creek.
scenes.headline: Kori Creek is born

scenes.narration: And on 26 January 2001, Republic Day, another earthquake hit near Bhuj, the main city of Kutch.
scenes.headline: Republic Day 2001

scenes.narration: So this land is still moving. Rivers, shorelines and creeks here are not fixed lines, and that matters for the last chapter.
scenes.headline: Land that moves

scenes.narration: The last chapter is about a creek two countries cannot agree on. But there is one more strange thing first.
scenes.headline: One more first

scenes.narration: Here is a thing about time. Your clock shows the same time in Kutch and in Arunachal Pradesh.
scenes.headline: Same clock

scenes.narration: But the sun does not agree. Kutch is in the far west and Arunachal is in the far east, so the sun reaches them almost two hours apart.
scenes.headline: Sun, two hours apart

scenes.narration: India uses one time, Indian Standard Time, across the whole country. So the sunrise in the east comes while Kutch is still dark.
scenes.headline: One time, one country

scenes.narration: In Kutch, the evening sun sets late by the clock, and it stays light long after the east has gone dark.
scenes.headline: Late sunsets

scenes.narration: It is one more way this corner of India feels like the edge of the map. And at the very edge, there is a creek.
scenes.headline: The edge of India

scenes.narration: Now the big one. Sir Creek. It is a narrow channel of water, about 96 kilometres long, in the marshes between Gujarat and Pakistan's Sindh.
scenes.headline: Sir Creek

scenes.narration: On a map, it looks like a thin blue crack running into the Arabian Sea. On the ground, it is mud, mangroves and tides.
scenes.headline: A crack in the map

scenes.narration: Patrols here often move by boat, because the land floods and the mud can swallow a boot.
scenes.headline: Patrols by boat

scenes.narration: So why do India and Pakistan disagree? Because one simple question has two answers: where exactly does the border run in this water?
scenes.headline: Where is the line?

scenes.narration: Is it along the eastern bank, which would give the whole creek to Pakistan? Or right down the middle of the water?
scenes.headline: Bank or middle?

scenes.narration: The story starts before 1947. Kutch was a princely state, and Sindh was part of British India, under the Bombay government.
scenes.headline: Before 1947

scenes.narration: In 1914, the Bombay government issued a resolution to settle a border argument between Sindh and the ruler of Kutch.
scenes.headline: The 1914 resolution

scenes.narration: That document has two paragraphs that seem to pull in different directions. One points toward the eastern bank.
scenes.headline: Two paragraphs

scenes.narration: The other uses a rule called the thalweg principle, which puts the border in the middle of the main navigable channel.
scenes.headline: Thalweg rule

scenes.narration: Thalweg is a German word for the line of the deepest channel. Creeks move, and the middle moves with them.
scenes.headline: The deepest line

scenes.narration: In the 1920s, pillars were placed along the creek's mid-channel, and a map from 1925 shows that line.
scenes.headline: The 1925 map

scenes.narration: India says that map settles it. The border is in the middle, and that is where India's claim stands.
scenes.headline: India's claim

scenes.narration: Pakistan says the thalweg rule should not apply, because in its view the creek is not navigable, so the east bank is the line.
scenes.headline: Pakistan's claim

scenes.narration: India disagrees. It says the creek is navigable for much of the year, so the mid-channel rule applies.
scenes.headline: Navigable or not?

scenes.narration: So both sides are reading from the same old papers, and both can point to a line in them.
scenes.headline: Same papers, two readings

scenes.narration: Now the part that sounds fake. The creek itself changes. Tides push mud, silt builds up, and channels shift over the years.
scenes.headline: The creek moves

scenes.narration: A border drawn in the middle of a channel is a border that wants to move when the channel moves.
scenes.headline: A moving middle

scenes.narration: That is the problem with water. A fence stays where you build it. A creek will not.
scenes.headline: Fences stay, creeks don't

scenes.narration: The creek is more than a few lines on a map. It also helps decide where the sea border begins.
scenes.headline: Sea border starts here

scenes.narration: Analysts say that where the land border meets the sea, a small shift in the line can change a large area of water.
scenes.headline: Small shift, big sea

scenes.narration: That water matters. It holds fishing grounds, and analysts say there may be oil and gas under the seabed too.
scenes.headline: Fish, oil and gas

scenes.narration: Fishermen feel the dispute the most. Boats drift across an invisible line, and crews on both sides have been arrested for it.
scenes.headline: Fishermen pay the price

scenes.narration: Out there, the line is not painted anywhere. A boat can cross it without anyone on board knowing.
scenes.headline: An invisible line

scenes.narration: Talks have gone on for decades. India and Pakistan have discussed Sir Creek in rounds of official talks, and it is still unresolved.
scenes.headline: Decades of talks

scenes.narration: It is in the news again. In recent years, Indian leaders have spoken sharply about Sir Creek and security in the area.
scenes.headline: Back in the news

scenes.narration: There is history here too. In 1965, a clash in the nearby Rann of Kutch led to fighting between the two countries.
scenes.headline: 1965 clash

scenes.narration: In 1968 a tribunal ruled on the Rann of Kutch border, but the dispute over Sir Creek never fully went away.
scenes.headline: 1968 tribunal

scenes.narration: So let us pull it together. Sir Creek is a border that depends on a word, a pillar, and a channel of water.
scenes.headline: Word, pillar, water

scenes.narration: Two old paragraphs, pillars from the 1920s, and a creek that moves. That is enough to keep a dispute alive for decades.
scenes.headline: Enough for decades

scenes.narration: So go back to the first line. Your Gujarat map hides a creek India and Pakistan still argue over, because the water keeps moving.
scenes.headline: Back to the start

scenes.narration: A salt desert that becomes a sea, swimming camels, a sign nobody can read, and a quake that built a wall.
scenes.headline: All in one corner

scenes.narration: All of that sits in one stretch of India, and all of it ends at one muddy creek.
scenes.headline: One muddy creek

scenes.narration: Next time: the country whose clocks run fifteen minutes ahead of India's. Watch it, and see how a clock can feel like a border.
scenes.headline: Next: the odd clock
